So the instructions were that whenever we found anything which might be interesting or be linked to any of these incidents or persons, that we have been listed, there has been the priorities, we took that, if it was -- if it had some relevance, according to our first evaluation. So it wasn't just going there and taking everything out and leaving. No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But as you didn't know the B/C/S language, and as these documents were in that language, how could you, on the basis of keywords, make a selection between interesting and less interesting documents? Who assisted you in reading the documents? Because a document consisting of a number of pages, it takes a few minutes to read it. So how did you proceed exactly?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: So you were right when you said that it really time-consuming task and we had -- I don't remember exactly investigators and analysts we had on that particular mission, but we had many of them and we had many language assistants. So we were working in pairs. Each investigator had their own interpreter, and they had been allocated certain area or certain shelves of the archive, which they went systematically, binder after binder, and they picked up all the relevant documents. Or if it turned out to be that, for example, a certain binder, that almost all of it seemed to be relevant, we took the whole binder, without reading every single document, that they were relevant, just to save time. And then the evidence was logged in the logbook, or log sheet, with all the details, describing the person who located it, from which archive it was, which archive room of a certain archive, which shelf, and if it was taken out of the binder, also the binder was mentioned, what's written in the spine of the binder, and these kind of details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I have understood this correctly, you were in the room, there were shelves, a binder, you had keywords, you knew that certain things might be of interest, you'd open the binder containing the documents. Did you or the interpreter or the assistant who knew B/C/S read the document? Did you read the document or did your assistant do this?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: The assistant, the interpreter or the language assistant, read the statement or whatever the document was. She had a kind of rough look what it contained and gave me a brief description what it contained. And then I made the decision whether that had some relevance or not. If it had, we took it; if not, we just went to the following document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before this operation, did you say, "We should look into documents called such-and-such, having such an ID number of the unit," and so on? Did you have some kind of a system of reading through these documents so that you could target the ones you were interested in?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes. Like I said earlier, that we were allocated certain shelves or parts of the archive, and most of the time the archive consisted -- it was built so that there were, for example, unit -- let's say 305, 306 Brigade. There was all the binders of that particular brigade were next to each other and in a kind of way that they were in a chronological order, starting from 1992, 1993, 1994, and so on. So we were able to go immediately to the certain binder that was of interest to us, and that's the way we proceeded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the local archivists, they collaborated with you fully, you had no problems with them regarding the reading of those documents and the taking of those documents? You never had any problems with them?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, we never had any problems. And at the end of each day, in the evening, we printed out the log sheet where we had listed all the documents and binders that we have taken. So we printed it out and get him to sign it. We left him a copy of the material that we have seized and one copy for ourself, one for the archivist, then we transported all the material after they were sealed and numbered and logged into the log sheet, we transported to the Sarajevo field office in a secured office room where they were kept until they were transported to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 12.30. We have to have the break now, and we will resume at about five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, I have no other questions for you, but another Judge will have a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: These are very small questions, but we had to make a break. So I'm going to put them now. The first question is the following: You explained your instructions to the Witness ZI in interviewing inhabitants of these villages where there have been destructions, and you said to him, if I understood you well: For each place, you specified the time period. For instance, for Dusina, you said January. For Miletici, you said April. For Guca Gora, June, et cetera. So for each specific village, you had a specific time frame. And if I remember well, these were always time frames of a month.

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes. It was the actual month when the village was attacked, whether it was in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The months in which the village was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah. Whether it was in the beginning or end, it didn't matter. Just the calendar month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Because there is a variation in that. In some situations the attack was at the end of the month, and in some situations it was rather at the beginning of the month.

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes, exactly what I said. So that was the decision made by the senior trial attorney and that's how we proceeded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But my question is: Why did you select a time period of a month? Why not a different yardstick? What were your considerations in doing it?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: I'm probably not the right person to answer for this. And there were certain discussions about what would be the simplest way and how we would do it, but anyway the decision made by him was that. It's the calendar month of the actual attack on each village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I didn't quite hear you. But someone in the OTP made the decision I understand.

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah. It was the senior trial attorney, Ekkehard Withopf, who made the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: He made the decision?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: It was before the mission, when we started to plan how we're going to proceed with this mission and how we're going to conduct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Have you had a discussion on that? If you don't want to answer this question, you don't have to, but have there been any discussions on yardsticks for selecting a period? Because you could imagine other periods, or other matters of selecting a period.

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm not in a position to remember exactly what was the discussions and what were the reasons for him for selecting this -- the way he selected. It's just the way he announced that it should be taken and that's how I passed on the information to our contact person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll put you no further questions on this issue. You said that you had also made pictures of individual houses and barns and other buildings, on average two for each building. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah. Each of the actual buildings, they were photographed from both sides so that we could see the whole building from both sides, from south and north, or east and west. And most of the outbuildings, we only took one. But for all the actual buildings, it was two for each.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And they are on CD-ROM?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: We have to look at them. The Prosecutor wants us to admit these CD-ROMs, but we haven't yet any -- had any possibility of looking at them. But let me just ask you: These pictures on CD-ROM of individual houses, have you indicated for each individual house also the owner or the former owner of the place or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah. We kept a log sheet, so each house has been numbered and we know exactly what time, which date the photo was taken, who took the photo, who is the owner of the house, from which direction it was taken. All this is logged and we have the binder with all the log sheets, and they are submitted as evidence to the system here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So they are easy to consult in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. My final question is more a question for the record, because there has been a discussion on the matter in March. Because the question has been raised in March, I raise it again here, and it's very easy for you to answer the question, I think. On the pictures you took, you have these signs in blue and red, red being houses, blue being other buildings. Say, for instance, you have 12 in red, that's a house, and 12 in blue, that's a barn belonging to the house. Now, in your sketches, you have obviously no blue and red, but you have different distinctions. You have, for instance, 12 and 12A. This is the same thing, the same revision, I understand?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. That was the way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Just for the record to make it absolutely clear that there's no difference between the documents in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Uh-huh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will go now to Defence counsel for questions that they may have following the questions of the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Further cross-examination by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Good day once again, Mr. Tauru. We have a few questions for you arising from the questions put to you by the Judges. The first question which I'd like to confirm with you is that the pictures that you took were taken in April of 2002, and you can confirm, of course, that they represent the situation of destruction in 2002?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can also confirm that the investigation in this case began as early as 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes. It had started a while before I arrived in September 1999, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you can also confirm that the relationship between the Office of the Prosecution and Witness ZI began with the same time as this investigation began?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: That I don't know, because I wasn't here when the investigation started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you confirm that this Witness ZI has been a contact of the Office of the Prosecution for the complete period during which you were an investigator with the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: As far as I recall, in the beginning when I joined the Tribunal, in the beginning there was actually another person officially. But as far as I understand, the actual job was anyway done by the ZI, or whatever the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Witness ZI?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah. But later on he, like, became the official contact person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you confirm, Mr. Tauru, that Witness ZI worked on only one type of crime or one type of alleged crime, and that is, crimes committed by Bosnian Muslims on Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, he also assisted some other teams with regard to crimes committed by the Serbs. But I'm not actually absolutely sure, but that's the picture in my mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Against Bosnian Croats as victims?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You had drawn up the sketches and that your source of information for the sketches and then of course to put the information on those pictures was Witness ZI; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think we have to go back into private session because one of the answers of the witness appeared during the open session. So we'll go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] So we were -- you just confirmed that your source of information was Witness ZI. Now, can you confirm that you don't know who Witness ZI contacted to gather this information which became your source of information?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: I know some names that he contacted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know some of the names, but there are many that you don't know. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those that you do know, you would not be surprised to know that they have appeared as witnesses before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people, whether you know them or you don't know them, and you just mentioned that most of them you don't know, can you confirm that you do not know where these people were in the particular month that you were looking for in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are not in a position to confirm whether these people, these subsources or third-hand sources, were eyewitnesses or not to the information that was provided to you?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be a fair assumption to say that because this was the war and that many people were fleeing their villages before the damage often took place, would it be a fair statement to say that there's a very likelihood that these people were not eyewitnesses to the damage that you were looking for?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: I'm not able to -- I don't want to speculate on that. But what I want to say, that some of the witnesses who gathered the information from the villages had been then later on interviewed by the OTP investigators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as I've said earlier, these witnesses have come to tell their stories before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, based on your experience, Mr. Tauru, I'd like to confirm that you are aware that some people used to burn their own property before leaving their villages in order to deprive the use of their buildings to whoever was taking their villages over. Are you aware of this fact, based on your 25 investigation missions in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, no other witness that I took a statement from mentioned anything like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to quickly -- you mentioned that when you visited some of these villages along with Witness ZI you mentioned that you had coffee with some people and that these people were Croats who had returned. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah, probably once, if I can recall, once or twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that these people knew very well Witness ZI. And they knew what he was looking for?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I move on to a different topic, and that is the village of Miletici. Because you mentioned something that was of particular interest. You mentioned that you saw a house in the year 2000, and then when you later were in the same village in 2002, this village looked totally different. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't know whether I mentioned these particular years, but anyway, there was about a year between the visits, and that particular house looked pretty much different from inside. So my idea kind of, you know, what I learned about this was that there's some kind of looting still going on or people are taking building material from those partly destroyed houses for their own purposes and some walls had been damaged there and kind of upper roof was taken out. And if I didn't know that I was in that particular part or house, I wouldn't have recognised it was the same one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, in the indictment against General Hadzihasanovic, there is one particular incident which took place in Miletici on the 25th of April, 1993. Now, the Defence position with respect to this incident is quite clear, is that whoever was there was not a member of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But what is more important is that witnesses who have appeared before this Trial Chamber have said that on this particular occasion, there was no damage whatsoever done to any of the houses. Now, if those witnesses are right in what they said before the Trial Chamber, under oath, of course, would it be a fair statement to say that the houses shown on your sketch as being destroyed, and I counted 12 of those, would have been destroyed at a different time frame?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Well, if the witnesses say so, according to the source that our contact person was able to locate and according to information he got from this person - I think it was a female - there was damage done to the village right after the village was attacked and taken over by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the -- talking about the issue of destruction in general, which was covered by the Presiding Judge, can you confirm that most houses in Bosnia, most houses which are damaged, have indeed bullet holes and that there are very few houses who do not have bullet holes in them? And you've been there many times.

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Well, I'm not really able to say if most of the houses have and most of them don't have. It depends a little bit on the area and what has happened in the area and whether there have been really actual fighting going on or just destruction after some villages have been taken over, whether there was any resistance or not. So it really depends on the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, can you confirm that when we talk about destruction of houses and, as a general, you have made -- you have visited the former Yugoslavia on 20 to 25 occasions. Can you confirm that when you were there in 2002, destruction is to be found everywhere in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah, pretty much so. Some area has been rebuilt, but there's still pretty much to be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you confirm, Witness, that the war in Central Bosnia, are you aware that this war lasted from 1992 to 1995, which is actually over a three-year period?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you confirm that throughout this period, there was a confrontation line, actually -- there were two confrontation lines; one between the Serb and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and one between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that these lines were there throughout the war, and of course they changed places wherever they would be close to some villages or not. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah, pretty much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the issue of destruction again which was raised by the Presiding Judge, you mentioned that the kind of destruction that you witnessed as an investigator would have to be done either by many people in a short time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Well, there are many possibilities. I just gave an example how it might happen. You know, one person can cause a lot of damage if he wants to do in one hour, setting 50 houses on fire, if needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So another possibility is less people over a longer period?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Less people, if they are active enough, in a short period as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And ten years later, it would be impossible to tell which of these options would take place, would have taken place?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Well, it's quite difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For both you and I, this would be pure speculation, would it be?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when we say groups, like many, small groups, big groups, that could be any group. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Group of soldiers, group of civilians, depending on --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Group of bandits?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: For example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Group of Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your sketches, in your testimony, you mentioned that there were 631 houses which had been destroyed, that you counted in your sketches. Now, I myself counted only 445. Are you sure about this figure that you are mentioning today?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: That figure is mentioned in the mission report that I prepared after the mission. There was something like 391 -- 391 buildings and 240 outbuildings, as far as I can recall now from the mission report I made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I count on these sketches admitted before this Trial Chamber, or at least that admission is being requested, I counted 393, that is, excluding Dusina, because the Prosecution has acknowledged the fact that there was no destruction charges any more for Dusina, and also Buhine Kuce, because that is a charge that is no longer relevant to this indictment. And I counted 393. Would that be a possibility, or in any event would the sketches reveal the right number?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm not really able to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a quick question on the looting. This is an issue that was also raised by the Presiding Judge. Can you confirm that on the basis of your experience -- now, when I talk about experience, I talk about your 20 to 25 trips in the region, but I also talk to your conversations with fellow investigators and with witnesses. Can you confirm that the looting in the former Yugoslavia basically had a pattern, where initially there was looting, whether it be by soldiers, civilians, criminals, of small items; a few days later, medium items; and then eventually the looting actually took the form of stealing windows, doors, roof tiles, pipes, where, in fact, at the end of the looting, after weeks and months and years, there was actually nothing left in these houses? Is that a pattern that you discussed and you were able to notice based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Well, there are cases like that. I'm definitely sure about that. But also I remember interviewing some witnesses who said that, you know, they started to carry those TV sets and VCRs right after the village was taken over. So it's also a question of case by case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A case-by-case situation?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Everything could have taken place. But the scenario I mentioned to you is a pattern that you have discussed and that you are aware of in some parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Well, I have heard about this kind of pattern being mentioned and probably at least one of the witnesses that I interviewed mentioned this very pattern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I move on to a question which was put to you by another one of the Honourable Judges of this Trial Chamber, and you confirmed that the idea of taking a time frame of a month, that was a decision which was made by a higher level within the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you confirm that within the Office of the Prosecution, that there have been times when you were there that lawyers were leading investigations, that there have been times at some places investigators have been leading investigations, and that when you were there, you can confirm that this has been an ongoing source of confusion and of discontent within the Office of the Prosecution during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: With all due respect, I really fail to see how this arises out of the Judges' questions, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Anyway, my answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think you had better let the President rule, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon. Could you rephrase the question, because that type of question was not put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will simply withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Witness, one last question I have for you today, and that is: The fact that -- well, actually, I have two questions. One is we mentioned something about the CD-ROMs having pictures of houses.

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that somewhere there was some information about owners and dates. Now, all this information, of course, again, is the result of your source, which is Witness ZI?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yes. But when we actually took the photographs, this ZI witness was not around. But it was based on, of course, on his information that he gave me, and the information which is now in the log sheets of those photographs. That's from my sketches. So actually he's anyway the original source of the names and buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My final question to you, Mr. Tauru, is that: You can confirm, of course, that this mission in April of 2002 actually took place after the initial appearance in the beginning of the proceedings, the pre-trial proceedings, against General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: I don't remember the dates, but that's possible, if you say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you confirm that as an investigator and member of an investigation team and involved in a specific case that it is the position of the Office of the Prosecution that when an accused is brought in for his Initial Appearance, they are actually trial ready and they have all the witnesses they need to take the case forward?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No, no. Please. Mr. President, please. I think it's unfair to ask this witness this question. This witness is an investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Regarding this type of question, we can't really see how the witness can provide an answer, because he wasn't the person who was providing the guidelines. He was executing instructions. But perhaps you could rephrase your question from another stand points. But Madam Benjamin is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the month and what you were --

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Sorry. I missed the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: The translation when you started to talk. So ask again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I will simply say my question in another form. Can you confirm that when those decisions were made and those decisions were communicated to you in terms of what you would be looking for and how you were to proceed on your mission, first, can you confirm that this took place after the Initial Appearance of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: I'm not sure when was the Initial Appearance of the accused, but it must have been before, so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you that the Initial Appearance of the accused took place in August of 2001 --

utterances.speaker: MIKA TAURU
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right. So it was after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my last question is simply: Usually when investigation teams proceed to do further work after a case has begun, it is to confirm and to strengthen their case, not to build a case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, well, well, well. I mean, Mr. President, my friend -- I think he knows better than that. Certainly this witness has no responsibility for the conduct of this case, and he knows that. So I don't understand why he insists on trying to get certain answers from this witness. This is not the witness. This is not the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence is only trying to demonstrate that in April 2002, the Prosecutor still didn't have a file, in spite of the fact that the accused had already been -- had already appeared and had already been indicted. But I withdraw my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll turn to the other Defence team. Perhaps they have some questions for this witness. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We don't have any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. Ms. Benjamin, now that the Defence has concluded its examination, is there anything else you would like to clarify with the witness, or do you have no further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Tauru, this concludes your testimony here. We would like to thank you for having come to testify here at the request of the Prosecution. You have answered all the questions put to you by the Prosecution, Defence, and the Judges that concerned your mission and investigation during the relevant time period. Thank you. And on behalf of the Judges, I wish you all the best in your difficult career as a police officer. And we wish you all the best in your new position, after having spent over three years working for the OTP. You now have a new job, and as I said, we wish you all the best in your new career. Thank you. And I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is almost time to adjourn, but there was an issue we had to deal with that concerned the documents under seal. We'll go into private session, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We have a few minutes left. Are there any comments to be made?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. With your leave, Mr. President, I would like to go back to the issue of the interviews taking place in Sarajevo at the moment, because I believe that some confusion remains with regard to how this is proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want to provide us with additional information or would you like the Prosecution to provide you with information?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to provide the Trial Chamber with information to clarify the situation, which remains, in my opinion, Mr. President, ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are listening to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Trial Chamber rendered an order requesting that the Prosecution call a witness who would testify about the drafting, the signing, and the forwarding of orders within the 3rd Corps. Having carried out a number of searches and a request of the assistance of the BH government, the only possible result was for the Prosecution to identify two Defence witnesses. Mr. President, these are witnesses -- these are two witnesses who have already been seen by the Defence, and they have agreed to testify about events for the Defence in the course of the Defence's case. Naturally, the Defence raise this issue before the Trial Chamber in order to avoid any problems or difficulties in relation to this subject. Mr. President and the Trial Chamber ruled and said that this was not a problem, as a witness is first and above all a witness in the interests of justice. The parties are in agreement. Nevertheless, the Prosecution, who is concerned about the rights of the accused, invited the Defence to attend the interviews with these witnesses who had already agreed to testify here. Mr. President, attending at -- being present at these interviews was important for a number of reasons. Firstly, in order to defend the accused's rights and to be aware of the contents of the discussion, and also for the well-being of the witnesses who might easily be confused, since they agreed to testify for the Defence and all of a sudden they're requested to go to the OTP office in Sarajevo for an interview in front of cameras. And the witnesses might have difficulty in understanding this. And thirdly, Mr. President, since we wanted someone to be present, someone familiar with the situation that was going to be discussed at the interviews, and these concerned questions of the authenticity of documents and how orders were drafted and forwarded in the 3rd Corps. And thirdly, Mr. President, as we always want to be fully prepared for hearings, we would like a person attending the interview to be present when these witnesses testify. As far as the schedule of the Prosecution is concerned, this week is isn't possible for my colleague and myself to be present in Sarajevo because the witness schedule for Wednesday, today's witness, and Friday's witnesses, witnesses for which it was necessary to make lengthy preparations, and we had already decided that I would examine these witnesses, whereas my colleague will be examining witnesses on Tuesday, Thursday, and Monday. And as far as I'm concerned, I had to deal with the issue of documents on Monday, at the beginning of the week. Given our work load, it's our opinion that it wouldn't be practical for my colleague or myself to go to Sarajevo this week. We have someone who is in Sarajevo. You know who this person is, Mr. President. It is Mrs. Mirna Milanovic, who is present here in The Hague from time to time. Nevertheless, Mr. President, although this person is a lawyer, she wasn't involved in the issue of documents, and this person can't be present, won't be able to be present when this witness is heard, if the witness is heard. As a result, we contacted the Registry last Wednesday to inform of a possible solution. To help, our legal assistant, Mr. Alexis Demirdjian, he could be prepared to help with the documents, and he could be present in Sarajevo and deal with all the problems. The Registry told us that this was a reasonable alternative and that this request would be accepted. That was on Wednesday. On Friday, Mr. President, we provided the necessary papers. The request for travel had been given to the Registry's travel department and reservations were made so that Mr. Demirdjian could travel to Sarajevo on Monday. On Friday afternoon, Mr. President, my colleague and myself spent the entire afternoon with the representatives from the Registry who had the responsibility to make such decisions. The deputy chief of the OLAD section, one of his colleagues, were present. We spent the entire afternoon with them and we were then present at a reception, and we met the Registrar, the Deputy Registrar, and these two persons. At no time in the course of that day, Mr. President, were we informed that a change had been made and that the request that we were making on Wednesday, which had been orally approved, we weren't informed that the reaction to the request was being amended. It was only on Friday, very late, that I learned that Mr. Alexis Demirdjian had been informed that his request had only been partially approved and that he had to pay for his own expenses when going to Sarajevo if he was to represent us there. So that was the weekend, Mr. President. We are faced with a fait accompli. We immediately wrote a letter to the person responsible in the Registry. We sent an email to the person responsible in the Registry, and we sent an email to the legal officer of the Chamber, as well as to the Prosecution. We sent the Prosecution an email which was received by Mr. Mundis, who immediately responded, saying that he understood the situation and that he understood that it was possible that this question, this issue could result in a delay with regard to the interviews, because we couldn't have our legal assistant going to Sarajevo if his expenses weren't covered, which is usually the case for all other representatives of the UN who are going on an official mission. On Monday morning, Mr. President - and I'm almost finished - on Monday morning we were informed that the decision had not been changed because it was the policy of the Registry not to pay for any trips for missions that involved legal assistants. In spite of what we were informed of the previous week, it is our opinion, unless we are mistaken, that there are no written policies with regard to this subject and that this only concerns a decision of an administrative official, and we believe that it is not a reasonable decision. As a result, Mr. President, we had to reserve tickets so that I could personally go to Sarajevo on two occasions this week. And I would like to confirm the fact that the Defence does not like going to Sarajevo and returning - I came back very late. I spent the night preparing for the witness. I'm going back to Sarajevo this afternoon, and I'll be ready for the witness on Friday morning. This is very expensive for the Registry. It is detrimental to the Defence preparations. And we believe, Mr. President, as I said a minute ago, that it is not a reasonable decision. Mr. President, the question raised before you on Monday was not a matter of asking for the Trial Chamber's assistance. We realised that the Trial Chamber's hands are tied as far as budgetary issues are concerned. Nevertheless, the reason for which the legal officer of the Chamber was informed in advance was that perhaps there was the possibility that might be necessary to delay the interviews, to delay the procedure. We wanted to avoid this. The only way of avoiding such a delay was to reserve two tickets so I could go on two return tickets to Sarajevo in the same week. Mr. President, the Trial Chamber ruled on Monday and said something about the necessity of the Defence going to Sarajevo to attend these interviews, so we agreed that the budgetary situation of the Tribunal is not a very agreeable situation to be in. If the Trial Chamber believes that this second trip to Sarajevo, which I'll be going on today, is not necessary, and if the Trial Chamber believes that the expense would be too great, I would not hesitate to cancel this trip. We want to act reasonably when spending public money. And nevertheless, Mr. President, as the Trial Chamber may have noted, we are professionals and we won't accept to be present at a hearing if we aren't completely prepared. We will prepare ourselves so that we can guarantee a full and professional defence for the accused. Mr. President, I wanted to provide you with these clarifications in order to avoid any confusion in relation to this subject, since we believe that we have acted in a reasonable way and that given the circumstances, it is necessary to deal with this issue, to raise this issue with the Registry and underline the fact that we are spending public money for no reason, whereas a simple administrative decision would have allowed a lawyer, a legal assistant, who has been officially assigned to the case to represent us in Sarajevo, and this would not have been detrimental to the case that we are involved in. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon, for your comments. As far as I personally am concerned, I agree with you and you are quite right with regard to everything that you have said. It seems that the problem arose because initially you were given a verbal agreement and last Friday a change was made to this agreement. You were thus placed in a very difficult situation, and naturally this involved costs which were superior to those that would have had to be covered if your assistant had gone there. Additionally, it was very tiring for you, since you had to go on return trips, and your work load is very great. So I can only agree with what you have said. In addition, you said - and you are well aware of this - that the Trial Chamber doesn't have any funds at its disposal. Naturally, if we had such a possibility, in order to ensure that the proceedings ran smoothly and that the accused were well represented, we would have naturally supported the request for your assistant to attend the interview between the witness and the representatives of the Prosecution. But as you have two roles - you're president of the lawyers' association as well - you could in that capacity inform the Registry of the problem, which is a serious problem, a real problem. And naturally, you have my personal support in this procedure. The problem arose because, unfortunately, the witness sought by the Prosecution was a witness that the Defence was going to call. So that's why the problem arose. If the situation had been the reverse, we wouldn't have had this problem. But unfortunately, or fortunately - I'm not quite sure how I'd put it - this was the witness concerned. If we had been informed of this in advance, we could have found another solution. A solution would have been to have this witness as a witness for the Prosecution with regard to this technical issue alone. But you would keep the witness as a Defence witness, to be heard subsequently, and the witness would only have been examined with regard to technical issues. But given the way the situation has developed, unfortunately you are the victim, because you are going to have to leave again, and we will be missing you in the courtroom tomorrow. Are there any other issues to be raised? If not -- Ms. Benjamin, is there anything that you would like to say, in the light of what Mr. Bourgon has just said?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, except for the fact that the documents, Prosecution 81 to 89, the Prosecution wishes to have same tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These documents have been marked for identification. As far as the request to have these documents into evidence, what would the Defence say? We'll listen to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll be brief. First of all, I'd like to confirm that, as far as I can remember, we hadn't requested that a witness come to authenticate the sketches, but we said that only a factual witness who was present in 1993 could come to authenticate photographs. An investigator couldn't do so. Our main argument, Mr. President, was that the photographs and the sketches in this case are not relevant because they depict a situation in 2002, and that has nothing to do with the situation that prevailed in 1993. And as a result, the sketches and the photographs aren't relevant in this case. Their irrelevance is such that Article 89(C) and (D) should be applicable and the probative value of these sketches is inferior to the prejudice that could be done to the accused. One might be given the impression of a large-scale destruction, whereas we have no idea about when this large-scale destruction may have been caused. I'll stop there, Mr. President. On numerous occasions we have repeated our arguments with regard to the photographs and the sketches. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there anything else that the Defence team would like to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No. I wish to repeat what Mr. Bourgon said. That has been our objection all along and we maintain that objection. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges will rule on the matter and we will render our decision with regard to the documents just referred to, 81 and 89. We will inform you whether they will remain marked for identification or whether we will give them final exhibit numbers. We have worked for a few extra minutes. I apologise to the interpreters, and I will see everyone tomorrow at the hearing at 9:00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of June, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 25
